sections.heading: Hero
sections.body: A mountain-valley climbing region around Briancon and Ailefroide, mixing bolted multi-pitches, sport crags, bouldering and alpine scenery.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body:
The Durance Valley / Hautes-Alpes entry is a region, not one crag. The useful planning frame is Briancon, Ailefroide and the surrounding alpine valleys, with climbing spread across granite, limestone and mountain terrain.

This is a destination for climbers who like variety: long bolted granite routes, sport sectors, bouldering and rest days that still feel high in the mountains.

sections.heading: History and context
warnings: No sourced history and context content found for this pass.

sections.heading: Rock and climbing character
sections.body:
Ailefroide is the clearest reference point here: long bolted multi-pitch routes on granite. The broader Durance Valley also brings limestone and sport-climbing terrain, so expect more variety than one rock type or one crag style.

Expect mountain tactics rather than single-crag simplicity. Aspect, altitude and weather can matter as much as grade.

sections.heading: Who it suits
sections.body: This region suits climbers who want a spread-out alpine base and are comfortable choosing objectives by conditions. It is especially relevant for multi-pitch climbers and sport climbers who want routes beyond a single roadside sector.
warnings: No sourced who it suits content found for this pass.

sections.heading: Grades and difficulty
sections.body: The supported grade detail is narrow but useful: many long bolted Ailefroide routes sit between F5a and F6c+. The file does not claim a region-wide grade range or total route count.

sections.heading: Season and conditions
sections.body: Spring, summer and autumn are the practical rock-climbing windows for this mountain-valley entry. Higher or colder objectives need current condition checks, and winter belongs outside this basic destination copy.

sections.heading: Gear and equipment
sections.body: Pack for the chosen objective. Sport days need normal sport gear; long bolted routes need multi-pitch kit, a comfortable descent plan and enough clothing for mountain weather shifts.
warnings: No sourced gear and equipment content found for this pass.

sections.heading: Transport and access
sections.body: A car is the conservative default because the climbing is spread across valleys and bases. Airport and public-transport details are worth checking for the exact base before relying on them for a trip plan.

sections.heading: Where to stay
sections.body: Campsites and apartments are sensible base options for a Briancon/Ailefroide-style trip. Choose named lodging close to the sectors you expect to use rather than treating the whole valley as one compact base.

sections.heading: Rest days
sections.body: Rest days can stay in the mountains: valley walks, Briancon logistics and low-effort days around Ailefroide all fit the character of the region.
warnings: No sourced rest days content found for this pass.

sections.heading: Practical tips
sections.body: Choose objectives by altitude and aspect. In a region this spread out, a good plan is often a weather plan: keep a lower sport option, a longer route option and a recovery day in reserve.
warnings: No sourced practical tips content found for this pass.

sections.heading: Safety notes
sections.body: Mountain weather, longer routes and descents are the main safety frame. Carry enough clothing, check descent information before committing and treat bolted multi-pitches as mountain days, not gym-style sport routes.
warnings: No sourced safety notes content found for this pass.

sections.heading: FAQ
sections.body:
Is this one crag? No. It is a regional entry around Briancon, Ailefroide and the Durance Valley.

What climbing style is strongest? Bolted multi-pitch climbing is a major part of the area, alongside sport climbing and bouldering.

Is a car needed? It is the practical default for this spread-out region.
